specs.overlay_big: EVERY FIX EXPOSES THE NEXT MESS
specs.scene: Overhead flat-lay of a hotel front-desk reception ledge, the working surface of the business itself: a paper reservation ledger lies open beside a fan of brass room-key tags, a stack of printed guest folios, a corded desk phone, a small room-service order pad, and a handful of blank comment cards, all pushed dense toward every frame edge and overlapping at the corners; two hands enter from the bottom edge mid-sort, one steadying the ledger, the other lifting a key tag, with bare patches of counter left between the objects.
specs.source_quote: the reservation fix exposed the inventory mess, the inventory fix exposed the reporting mess

recognisable.why: a hotel front desk with room keys and a reservation ledger reads instantly as a familiar trade without any label.

legibility.why: ledger, keys, phone, order pad and cards are five separately resolvable elements, well past the three-element cutoff.

curiosity.why: the phrase implies an unending chain of hidden problems the viewer cannot see the end of, though it is close to a plain description.

subject.why: there is no single anchor person or object — the point of the shot is the scatter itself.

credible.why: no figure is carried, which the rubric scores as full credit.

stakes.why: implies ongoing maintenance burden for anyone who takes this work, a real but secondary risk to the viewer.

reexpress.why: introduces the chain-reaction consequence the title never mentions, rather than repeating its dollar figures.

specs.overlay_big: NOT SCOPE CREEP. THE BUSINESS MODEL.
specs.scene: A documentary photograph of a hotel front-desk clerk at the reception counter, mid-conversation with an unseen guest, one hand resting on a closed reservation ledger and the other holding a room key out across the counter; the counter surface is otherwise plain, the clerk's uniform unbranded, the background a blurred lobby wall left positively blank.
specs.source_quote: That's not scope creep. That's the business model.

recognisable.why: a hotel clerk at a front desk is an immediately familiar trade scene, though it is a generic occupation rather than a named brand.

legibility.why: one person and one counter form a single readable mass, with only minor secondary detail in the ledger and key.

curiosity.why: this is the exact register-lane pattern of a flat editorial verdict over a documentary photo with no number, leaving the viewer wanting to know how it is engineered.

subject.why: the clerk mid-handoff is one clear human anchor performing one legible action.

credible.why: the caption carries no figure at all, which scores full.

stakes.why: the claim is about business structure rather than a direct threat or gain to the viewer, so relevance is present but indirect.

reexpress.why: the verdict about intentional scope creep is nowhere in the title and reframes the mechanism as strategy, not description.

specs.overlay_big: COST OF GOODS ROUNDS TO ZERO
specs.scene: A single unbranded countertop card reader and receipt printer sitting on a stainless restaurant counter, cables resting neatly behind it, a till drawer cracked open just beside it, the counter surface otherwise bare and reflective, no person in frame.
specs.source_quote: cost of goods on a two thousand dollar project rounds to zero

recognisable.why: a card reader and till on a counter are everyday objects any viewer identifies instantly without context.

legibility.why: one object dominates the frame with nothing else competing for separate resolution.

curiosity.why: the line reads as a settled economic fact rather than a verdict the viewer is left wanting to resolve, so it under-delivers on this dimension.

subject.why: the card reader is a single distinctive object anchor, exactly what this dimension rewards.

credible.why: no dollar figure appears in the overlay itself, so it scores full by the rubric's own rule.

stakes.why: a near-zero cost of goods speaks directly to the viewer's own risk of entry.

reexpress.why: this margin detail is absent from all three titles and adds a consequence the title does not carry.

specs.scene: Close crop on a pair of hands mounting a small tablet order-terminal onto a bracket at a restaurant kitchen pass, screen face left positively blank, a loose cable still hanging beneath the mount, stainless pass surface visible and clean to the left of the action for the overlay.
specs.source_quote: if it's that easy, why is Accenture charging billions for it?

recognisable.why: hands mounting a tablet at a kitchen pass reads as workplace installation but is less iconic than a named brand or singular object.

legibility.why: hands and the single device form one dominant mass with only the loose cable as minor secondary detail.

curiosity.why: the line implies an unresolved 'hard part' the viewer cannot see, echoing the source question about why this stays expensive at scale.

subject.why: a person mid-action installing one distinct object is exactly the anchor this dimension asks for.

credible.why: the overlay carries no figure, scoring full.

stakes.why: directly implies the viewer could attempt this themselves, which is a personal gain/threat frame rather than market trivia.

reexpress.why: the difficulty claim is not in any of the three titles and adds a consequence beyond their dollar framing.
